You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

Explain how the proposed framework in the above text relates to python code snippets.

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

name: read
content:
1	Adverse Drug Reactions (ADRs) are a leading cause of hospital admissions and healthcare costs.
     2	Traditional methods of ADR reporting often rely on post-marketing surveillance, and manual reporting
     3	of ADRs to the local or national pharmacovigilance agencies for causality assessment and final
     4	reporting to the WHO. High-income countries have their own national (i.e., USFDA) and regional
     5	(i.e., European Medicines Agency / EMA) pharmacovigilance agencies. However, this process is slow
     6	and inefficient. This article proposes a novel framework for integrating ADR detection into clinical
     7	workflows using Electronic Medical Record (EMR) systems, crowdsourced reporting from patients and
     8	healthcare professionals, and graph theory for generating automated ADR signals and reports to the
     9	local or national pharmacovigilance agencies. The system leverages automated data collection from
    10	EMRs (drug prescriptions, clinical notes) by EMR data scraping, integrating ADR dictionaries and
    11	drug databases to automate the generation of ranked ADR signals. By applying graph theory, the
    12	system filters and upranks connections between drugs and ADRs, considering the temporal relationship
    13	between drug administration and ADR occurrence. This automated approach offers a significant
    14	improvement in ADR reporting, enabling faster detection and more accurate predictions.
    15	Methodologies, framework visualizations and python code snippets are included to aid implementation.

According to `doc.txt`, the relationship is that the article includes python code snippets as part of its materials to help implement the proposed framework. The document states:

- The article "proposes a novel framework for integrating ADR detection into clinical workflows using Electronic Medical Record (EMR) systems, crowdsourced reporting from patients and healthcare professionals, and graph theory for generating automated ADR signals and reports to the local or national pharmacovigilance agencies" (doc.txt).
- "Methodologies, framework visualizations and python code snippets are included to aid implementation." (doc.txt)

That is the full extent of what the document says: the python code snippets are included alongside methodologies and framework visualizations to aid implementation of the framework. The document does not describe the content of the snippets or any other specific role they play.
